titrationSchedule.title: STEP 1
titrationSchedule.directive: Verification · Opioid-Free Screening Safety Verification Verify patient has been completely opioid-free for >= 7–10 days (or negative urine opioid im­ munoassay).

titrationSchedule.title: STEP 2
titrationSchedule.directive: Protocol · 18 mg PO 1–2 Hours Pre-Risk Target Dosing Patient takes 1 tablet on days when they anticipate a high risk of drinking, ideally 1–2 hours prior to first drink.

titrationSchedule.title: STEP 3
titrationSchedule.directive: In­ gestion Rule · Take Immedi­ ately if Drinking Started Damage Control If patient begins drinking without taking the tablet, they must take 1 tablet immediately to curb total alcohol intake. CRITICAL DRUG-DRUG INTERACTIONS & WARNINGS High-Risk Polypharmacy Opioid Analgesics (Complete Analgesic Blockade & Withdrawal) Nalmefene completely blocks the analgesic effects of all opioids (Morphine, Oxycodone, Fentanyl) and precipitates immediate, violent withdrawal in opioid- dependent patients; strictly contraindicated. Acute Surgical Anesthesia Protocols If emergency surgery is required in a patient on nalmefene, conventional opioid analgesics will fail; anesthesia must utilize regional blocks, ketamine, or non- opioid multimodal protocols.

clinicalPearls: Nalmefene is designed for 'as-needed' (targeted) dosing: the patient takes the medication only on days when they foresee a high risk of alcohol consumption, putting the patient in control and drastically reducing heavy drinking days.

Unlike Naltrexone (which carries an FDA Black Box warning for dose-dependent hepatocellular injury at high doses), Nalmefene is primarily glucuronidated and is not hepatotoxic, making it much safer in patients with mild-to-moderate alcoholic liver disease.

The FDA recently approved an intranasal formulation of Nalmefene (*Opvee* 2.7 mg) specifically for reversing synthetic fentanyl overdoses; because nalmefene has a 12-hour half-life, it prevents the delayed re-narcotization that occurs when short-acting naloxone wears off.

titrationSchedule.title: STEP 1
titrationSchedule.directive: En­ cephalopathy Loading · 30–45 mL PO/NG every 1–2 Hours Acute Clearing Administer hourly until initial bowel evacuation is achieved; in deep coma, administer as retention enema (300 mL in 700 mL water).

titrationSchedule.title: STEP 2
titrationSchedule.directive: Titration · 15– 30 mL PO TID to QID Clinical Calibration Adjust dose dynamically. The strict clinical goal is *2 to 3 soft, semi-formed bowel movements per day*.

titrationSchedule.title: STEP 3
titrationSchedule.directive: Avoidance Rule · Hold if > 3–4 Stools/Day Safety Boundary If patient has > 3 watery stools per day, hold dose temporarily and reduce maintenance to prevent hypokalemic alkalosis. CRITICAL DRUG-DRUG INTERACTIONS & WARNINGS High-Risk Polypharmacy Severe Diarrhea & Hypokalemia (Worsening Hepatic Encephalopathy) Over-titrating lactulose produces profound dehydration and hypokalemic meta­ bolic alkalosis. Alkalosis shifts circulating ammonium (NH4+) back into neutral ammonia gas (NH3), which rapidly crosses the blood-brain barrier and paradoxi­ cally worsens coma! Non-Absorbable Antacids (Magnesium Hydroxide) Antacids raise colonic luminal pH, neutralizing lactulose acidification and abol­ ishing the ammonia-trapping mechanism.

clinicalPearls: The clinical endpoint of Lactulose therapy is NOT watery diarrhea—it is *precisely 2 to 3 soft, semi-formed bowel movements per day*. Excessive diarrhea causes dehydration, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis, and paradoxically worsens hepatic encephalopathy.

In patients in deep hepatic coma (Grade 3–4) who cannot swallow, never force oral syrup (extreme aspiration pneumonitis hazard); administer Lactulose as a retention enema (300 mL Lactulose mixed with 700 mL water, retained for 30–60 minutes in Trendelenburg position).

If the excessively sweet syrup causes intractable nausea, switch to *Kristalose* (pure lactulose powder for oral solution dissolved in cold water or apple juice), which is significantly better tolerated.

titrationSchedule.title: STEP 1
titrationSchedule.directive: Prophylaxis Initiation · 550 mg PO BID with or without Food Standard Maintenance Initiate immediately following hospital discharge for an acute episode of overt hepatic en­ cephalopathy.

titrationSchedule.title: STEP 2
titrationSchedule.directive: tion with Lactulose · Add to Baseline Lactulose Regimen Combination Protocol Rifaximin is an *add-on* to lactulose; do NOT dis­ continue lactulose when starting rifaximin unless diarrhea is intolerable.

titrationSchedule.title: STEP 3
titrationSchedule.directive: Continu­ ous Mainte­ nance · 550 mg PO BID Indefinitely Sustained Prophylaxis Maintain continuous daily therapy indefinitely or until successful orthotopic liver transplantation. CRITICAL DRUG-DRUG INTERACTIONS & WARNINGS High-Risk Polypharmacy P-Glycoprotein Inhibitors (Cyclosporine, Verapamil) Co-administration with potent P-gp inhibitors (Cyclosporine) can modestly in­ crease systemic absorption of rifaximin (up to 80-fold increase, though still clinically safe); monitor Child-Pugh C patients. Zero Major CYP450 Drug Interactions Unlike systemic rifamycins (Rifampin), Rifaximin does not induce hepatic CYP3A4 at therapeutic doses due to minimal systemic absorption; it does not alter levels of transplant immunosuppressants or psychotropics.

clinicalPearls: In patients with cirrhosis and recurrent hepatic encephalopathy, adding Rifaximin 550 mg BID to standard Lactulose therapy reduces 6-month hospital readmissions by nearly 60% and significantly improves quality of life.
Never discontinue Lactulose when starting Rifaximin; randomized clinical trials (Bass et al., NEJM) demonstrated superiority of *combination therapy* (Rifaximin + Lactulose) over either agent alone.

Rifaximin acts strictly as a 'luminal disinfectant': by suppressing urease-producing enteric bacteria (which cleave urea into ammonia and CO2), it drastically diminishes the daily production of absorbable ammonia in the gastrointestinal tract.

titrationSchedule.title: STEP 1
titrationSchedule.directive: gency TdP Bolus · 2 g IV Push over 1–2 Minutes Immediate Resuscitation Administer 2 g IV push immediately upon identi­ fying Torsades de Pointes, *regardless of baseline serum magnesium*.

titrationSchedule.title: STEP 2
titrationSchedule.directive: Emergency Bolus · Re­ peat 2 g IV in 5–15 Min­ utes Refractory Arrhythmia If polymorphic VT recurs or persists, administer a second 2 g IV bolus; ensure continuous ECG telemetry.

titrationSchedule.title: STEP 3
titrationSchedule.directive: Maintenance Infusion · 2–4 mg/min Con­ tinuous IV Post-Crisis Infusion Initiate continuous maintenance infusion (diluted in D5W or 0.9% NaCl) for 24 hours to prevent delayed arrhythmia recurrence. CRITICAL DRUG-DRUG INTERACTIONS & WARNINGS High-Risk Polypharmacy Neuromuscular Blockers (Succinylcholine, Rocuronium) Magnesium potently enhances both depolarizing and non-depolarizing neuro­ muscular blockade, producing prolonged, unexpected flaccid paralysis and pro­ longed postoperative apnea. Hypermagnesemia Emergency Antidote (IV Calcium Gluconate) If severe magnesium toxicity occurs (loss of reflexes, respiratory depression), immediately administer 1 g IV Calcium Gluconate (10 mL of 10% solution) over 3 minutes to directly antagonize magnesium at the motor endplate.

clinicalPearls: In acute Torsades de Pointes, administer Magnesium Sulfate 2 g IV push *immediately*, even if the patient's baseline serum magnesium level is completely normal (e.g. 2.1 mg/dL); magnesium terminates TdP via pharmacologic calcium gating, not merely electrolyte repletion.

Always check the patellar deep tendon reflex (DTR) at the bedside during continuous IV magnesium infusions; the *loss of deep tendon reflexes* occurs at 8 to 10 mg/dL and serves as an early clinical warning before respiratory arrest occurs at > 12 mg/dL.

Hypokalemia cannot be successfully corrected until hypomagnesemia is concurrently corrected; magnesium is a required cofactor for the Na+/K+ ATPase pump and inhibits the renal ROMK channel that wastes potassium into urine.

titrationSchedule.title: STEP 1
titrationSchedule.directive: nique Instruc­ tion · 1 Drop Under the Tongue at Bedtime Initial Local Dosing Use standard 1% ophthalmic solution; instruct pa­ tient to tilt head back, place 1 drop strictly under tongue, and hold for 2–3 min.

titrationSchedule.title: STEP 2
titrationSchedule.directive: Escala­ tion for Severe Drooling · 2 Drops SL (or 1 Drop Each Side) Dose Optimization If wet-pillow symptoms persist after 3 nights, in­ crease to 2 drops sublingually at bedtime (1 drop on each side of frenulum).

titrationSchedule.title: STEP 3
titrationSchedule.directive: vs Swallow Technique · Spit Excess Saliva after 5 min Systemic Minimization Instruct patient to spit out residual pooled saliva after 5 minutes to prevent swallowing and sys­ temic GI absorption. CRITICAL DRUG-DRUG INTERACTIONS & WARNINGS High-Risk Polypharmacy Swallowed Drops & Clozapine Constipation (Fatal Ileus Hazard) If the patient swallows multiple drops instead of holding them sublingually, sys­ temic absorption produces additive antimuscarinic bowel paralysis with Clozapine, precipitating catastrophic fecal impaction and fatal bowel necrosis. Angle-Closure Glaucoma (Absolute Contraindication) Systemic antimuscarinics are strictly contraindicated in untreated narrow-angle glaucoma; pupillary dilation blocks the trabecular meshwork, causing acute blind­ ing intraocular pressure spikes.

clinicalPearls: Sublingual 1% Atropine ophthalmic drops represent the most elegant, targeted treatment for Clozapine nocturnal sialorrhea because they act locally on submandibular and sublingual salivary glands with minimal systemic absorption, avoiding the severe constipation caused by oral anticholinergic pills.

Prescribe the medication as standard *Atropine Sulfate 1% Ophthalmic Solution*, but instruct the patient and nursing staff to administer it *strictly sublingually under the tongue*—never into the eye.

To prevent the bitter taste of atropine from triggering nausea or non-adherence, place the 1–2 drops on a clean spoon or cotton swab, or mix with a drop of honey or syrup placed directly under the tongue immediately before sleep.

protocols.switchType: MODERATE CROSS-TAPER
protocols.classTransition: Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitor (SSRI) → Serotonin-Norepinephrine Reuptake Inhibitor (SNRI)
protocols.rationale: Clinical Rationale for SSRI to SNRI Rotation: Indicated for partial response or treatment-resistant depression with prominent fatigue, executive apathy, or comorbid neuropathic pain (fibromyalgia, diabetic peripheral neuropathy). Adding norepinephrine reuptake inhibition (NET) provides noradrenergic drive in prefrontal cortical networks while sustaining SERT occupancy.

phases.notes: Initiate SNRI at entry dose (Venlafaxine XR 37.5 mg or Duloxetine 30 mg) Days 1 to 7 (Week 1) Maintain dual therapy; monitor for mild transient nausea and mild headache. Verify baseline blood pressure.

phases.notes: Increase SNRI to therapeutic dose (Venlafaxine XR 75 mg or Duloxetine 60 mg) Days 8 to 14 (Week 2) Norepinephrine transporter (NET) recruitment begins. Assess for emergence of tremor, diaphoresis, or anxiety.

protocols.warning: BLOOD PRESSURE MONITORING MANDATE WITH VENLAFAXINE Venlafaxine inhibits the norepinephrine transporter (NET) in a dose-dependent fashion, with substantial noradrenergic tone emerging at doses ≥150 mg/day. A sustained increase in resting diastolic blood pressure (3–7 mmHg) occurs in up to 13% of patients at doses > 225 mg/day. Check baseline blood pressure prior to cross-titration and at weeks 2, 4, and 8.

protocols.title: Paroxetine Salvage & Fluoxetine Bridge
protocols.transitionTitle: Paroxetine → Other SSRI/SNRI / Fluox­ etine Bridge
protocols.switchType: CLINICAL PROTOCOL · PAROXETINE SALVAGE & FLUOXETINE BRIDGE (1/2) · Page 16
protocols.classTransition: Short Half-Life Anticholinergic SSRI → Alternative Antidepressant or Self-Taper Bridge
protocols.rationale: Why Paroxetine Causes Severe FINISH Syndrome: Paroxetine combines high SERT affinity (𝐾𝑑= 0.07 nM) with potent muscarinic 𝑀1 antagonism (𝐾𝑑= 72 nM) and autoinhibitory CYP2D6 kinetics (𝑡1 2 = 21 hours). Rapid down-titration triggers a catastrophic dual crisis: sudden cholinergic rebound alongside acute serotonergic uncoupling (‘brain zaps’ and vertigo). The Norfluoxetine Rescue Bridge Logic: When patients cannot tolerate Paroxetine reductions below 10–20 mg/ day due to electric shocks and panic, introducing a short 5-to-7 day bridge of Fluoxetine 20 mg daily provides an elegant biological solution. Norfluoxetine (𝑡1 2 = 7 −15 days) creates an imperceptibly smooth 5-week self-taper.

phases.title: Hyperbolic High-Dose Step-Down · Reduce Paroxetine from 40 mg to 30 mg daily (or 30 mg → 20 mg)
phases.notes: → Optional: Initiate incoming SSRI at 25% dose or none Days 1 to 14 (Weeks 1–2) Maintain for 14 full days to allow 2D6 de-saturation. Prescribe PRN Promethazine 25 mg qHS if nausea emerges.

phases.title: Low-Dose Step-Down & Anticholinergic Shield · Reduce Paroxetine from 20 mg to 10 mg daily →
phases.notes: Initiate Trihexyphenidyl 1–2 mg BID (or Promethazine 25 mg bedtime) Days 15 to 28 (Weeks 3–4) Critical vulnerability phase. If severe electric shocks appear, proceed directly to Phase 3 Fluoxetine Bridge.

phases.title: The Fluoxetine Rescue Bridge Initiation · Reduce Paroxetine to 5 mg for 3 days, then stop
phases.timing: completely (Day 32) → Administer Fluoxetine 20 mg PO daily in the morning
phases.notes: Days 29 to 35 (Week 5: 7 Days Total) Fluoxetine immediately captures uncoupled SERT sites. Maintain Fluoxetine for strictly 5 to 7 days.

phases.title: Abrupt Fluoxetine Cessation & Asymptotic Washout · Zero (Paroxetine fully eliminated) → Stop Fluox­
phases.timing: etine completely without further tapering (Day 36 onward)
phases.notes: Weeks 6 to 10 (Self-Taper) Norfluoxetine blood levels decay at ~5% per day over 35 days, eliminating discontinuation symptoms.

protocols.warning: DO NOT USE ALTERNATE-DAY PAROXETINE DOSING Instructing patients to take Paroxetine ‘every other day’ (e.g. 10 mg QOD) during the final stage is clinically disastrous. Because Paroxetine’s half-life is roughly 21 hours, blood levels plunge by > 75% on the skipped day, subjecting the patient to recurrent cholinergic rebound and panic every 48 hours. Always use smaller daily doses.

protocols.title: Fluoxetine Washout & Transitions
protocols.switchType: CLINICAL PROTOCOL · FLUOXETINE WASHOUT & TRANSITIONS (1/2) · Page 18
protocols.classTransition: Long-Acting SSRI / Potent CYP2D6 Inhibitor → Alternative Antidepressant Class or Irreversible MAOI
protocols.rationale: Why Fluoxetine Violates Standard Cross-Tapering Rules: Fluoxetine has an elim­ ination half-life of 2–4 days, but its active metabolite, Norfluoxetine, has an elimination half-life of 7 to 15 days. Complete metabolic clearance (5 × 𝑡1 2) requires 35 to 45 days (5 to 6 weeks). Adding a second antidepressant at full therapeutic dose while Norfluoxetine remains at 60–80% plasma concentrations produces severe pharmacokinetic accumulation and serotonin excess. The Two Divergent Transition Pathways: • Pathway A (Switching to Non-MAOI SSRI/SNRI/TCA): Stop Fluoxetine; wait 4–7 days drug-free; start new agent at low starting dose; titrate over 3–4 weeks. n• Pathway B (Switching to Irreversible MAOI): Stop Fluox­ etine; wait 5 FULL WEEKS (35 DAYS) drug-free before first MAOI dose. Zero exceptions!

If an MAOI is introduced while residual SERT reuptake pump blockade persists (from an SSRI, SNRI, or Clomipramine), intrasynaptic serotonin concentrations surge expo­ nentially by 1,000% to 5,000%. This floods postsynaptic 5 −HT1𝐴 and 5 −HT2𝐴 receptors, triggering fulminant, fatal hyperpyrexic Serotonin Toxicity. Mandatory Drug-Free Intervals: • Fluoxetine: Strict 5 WEEKS (35 DAYS) drug-free wait. n• Vortioxetine / Clomipramine: Strict 3 WEEKS (21 DAYS) wait. n• Sertraline, Citalopram, Paroxetine, SNRIs: Strict 2 WEEKS (14 DAYS) wait. n• Other TCAs (Nor­ triptyline, Amitriptyline): Strict 2 WEEKS (14 DAYS) wait.

protocols.rationale: The Rebound Storm Mechanism: Olanzapine and Quetiapine exert profound antag­ onism at muscarinic 𝑀1 and histaminergic 𝐻1 receptors with moderate-to-low 𝐷2 affinity. Switching to Aripiprazole or Cariprazine (negligible 𝑀1 𝐻1 affinity, high 𝐷2 par­ tial agonism) triggers a dual crisis: severe cholinergic rebound (nausea, diaphoresis, diarrhea) and catastrophic histaminergic insomnia, alongside net dopamine activa­ tion. Receptor Divergence Parameters: • Olanzapine: 𝐾𝑖 for 𝑀1 = 1.9 nM, 𝐻1 = 7 nM, 𝐷2 = 11 nM (𝑡1 2 = 33h). n• Quetiapine: 𝐾𝑖 for 𝐻1 = 11 nM, 𝛼1 = 94 nM, 𝐷2 = 380 nM (𝑡1 2 = 7h). n• Arip­ iprazole: 𝐾𝑖 for 𝐷2 = 0.34 nM, 𝑀1 > 1000 nM (𝑡1 2 = 75h). n• Cariprazine: 𝐷3 -preferring partial agonist (𝑡1 2 = 2 −4 days, DDCAR: 1–3 weeks).

If the antagonist is tapered before the partial agonist achieves therapeutic steady state, incoming dopamine and partial agonist molecules stimulate supersensitive receptors, trigger­ ing violent withdrawal akathisia and explosive rebound psychosis. Replaces 21 days of oral overlap! n• Risperdal Consta: 21-day PLGA silent lag; mandatory 21 days oral overlap.

protocols.rationale: Why Clozapine Cannot Be Tapered Quickly: Clozapine exhibits an unmatched, broad receptor binding profile: potent muscarinic 𝑀1 𝑀4 antagonism, 𝐻1 antagonism, 𝛼1-adrenergic blockade, and fast-off low-affinity 𝐷2 binding (𝐾𝑖= 125 nM). Re-exposing the patient to Clozapine produces an accelerated, fulminant, and frequently fatal immune-mediated bone marrow aplasia. The patient must be registered as permanently discontinued in the national REMS registry.

protocols.rationale: The UGT2B7 Glucuronidation Hazard: Lamotrigine clearance depends almost entirely on hepatic glucuronidation mediated by UDP-glucuronosyltransferase (UGT2B7 / UGT1A4). Co- prescribing Valproate more than doubles Lamotrigine elimination half-life (from 24 hours to > 60 hours) and doubles serum concentrations, dramatically elevating the risk of Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS) and toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN). Glucuronidation Dosing Paradigms: • Lamotrigine Monotherapy: W1–2: 25 mg/d → W3–4: 50 mg/d → W5: 100 mg/d → Target: 200 mg/d. n• With Valproate (Inhibitor): W1–2: 25 mg QOD → W3–4: 25 mg/d → W5: 50 mg/d → Target: 100 mg/d. n• With Carbamazepine (Inducer): W1–2: 50 mg/d → W3–4: 100 mg/d → Target: 400 mg/d.

protocols.rationale: Why Direct Tapering Fails: Short-acting high-potency benzodiazepines (Alprazolam, Lorazepam) have rapid clearance and sharp peak-trough fluctuations. Patients expe­ rience severe inter-dose withdrawal anxiety, tremor, and panic every 4 to 6 hours, rendering direct milligram step-downs virtually intolerable. Converting to Diazepam (𝑡1 2 = 20 −50h, active desmethyldiazepam 𝑡1 2 = 36 −200h) provides a completely smooth, continuous GABA-A receptor occupancy curve. Rushing the taper causes severe patient distress, emergency room visits, and reinstatement of higher doses. A 6-month taper is clinically superior.

protocols.rationale: The Rebound Insomnia Trap: Z-drugs (Zolpidem, Zopiclone, Eszopiclone) selectively target GABA-A receptors containing the 𝛼1 subunit. With chronic nightly use, 𝛼1 subunits down-regulate, producing pharmacodynamic tolerance, daytime anxiety, and severe rebound insomnia on discontinuation. Patients mistakenly interpret this violent rebound insomnia as proof of incurable underlying insomnia, leading to indefinite, years-long hypnotic dependence. Hypnotic Half-Lives & Rebound Kinetics: • Zolpidem (Ambien): 𝑡1 2 = 2.5 hours; ultra-short; severe middle-of-the- night awakening. n• Zopiclone (Imovane): 𝑡1 2 = 5.0 hours; metallic taste, intermediate duration. n• Eszopiclone (Lunesta): 𝑡1 2 = 6.0 hours; active S- enantiomer. n• Zaleplon (Sonata): 𝑡1 2 = 1.0 hour; rapid sleep onset only.

protocols.title: Alpha-2 Agonists & Rebound Hypertensive Crisis
protocols.switchType: Cross-Titration

protocols.coreMandate: NEVER Discontinue Centrally-Acting Alpha-2 Agonists Abruptly
protocols.rationale: The Rebound Hypertensive Storm Mechanism: Chronic administration of central 𝛼2-adrenergic agonists (Clonidine, Guanfacine) stimulates presynaptic inhibitory autoreceptors in the brainstem nucleus tractus solitarius, suppressing central sympa­ thetic outflow and down-regulating peripheral vascular receptors. Abrupt cessation removes this central brake overnight: a massive uninhibited surge of circulating catecholamines (epinephrine, norepinephrine) floods peripheral alpha-1 and beta-1 receptors, causing malignant hypertension, tachycardia, cerebral hemorrhage, and death. Rebound Kinetics & Elimination Half-Lives: • Clonidine (Catapres): 𝑡1 2 = 12 −16 hours; short duration; rebound crisis peaks within 18 to 36 hours of omission. n• Guanfacine (Intuniv): 𝑡1 2 = 17 hours; highly selective 𝛼2𝐴 agonist; slower rebound onset (36–72 hours). n• Transdermal Clonidine (TTS): Reservoir lasts 7 days; patch removal produces slow plasma decline over 48 hours.

Withdrawing Clonidine while beta-blockers remain active leaves massive circulating norepinephrine unopposed at alpha-1 vascular receptors, precipitating catastrophic hypertensive intracranial hemorrhage. protocols.rationale: The Precipitated Withdrawal Mechanism: Buprenorphine possesses a sub- nanomolar affinity for the mu-opioid receptor (𝐾𝑖= 0.2 nM), which is vastly higher than Methadone, Oxycodone, or Fentanyl, but exhibits low intrinsic efficacy (partial agonism). Administering standard Buprenorphine doses while full agonists still occupy mu receptors causes instantaneous displacement of full agonists, plunging opioid receptor activation from 100% to 30% within minutes—triggering violent precipitated withdrawal.
